title: THE HOLIDAY JESUS NEVER COMMANDED: ARE WE HONORING GOD… OR DEFENDING TRADITIONS HE NEVER ASKED FOR?
paragraphs: THE HOLIDAY JESUS NEVER COMMANDED: ARE WE HONORING GOD… OR DEFENDING TRADITIONS HE NEVER ASKED FOR?

Christmas. Easter. Holy Week. Religious celebrations passed down through generations. But what happens when a sincere Christian opens the Bible and discovers that some of the holidays they have celebrated all their lives were never explicitly commanded by Jesus? Is celebrating them an act of worship—or could refusing them become another form of religious pride? The answer may expose something far deeper than the dates on our calendars.
There is a kind of spiritual discomfort that begins with one innocent question.
“Where does the Bible actually command Christians to celebrate this?”
At first, the room becomes quiet.
Someone says, “We have always celebrated it.”
Another answers, “But it is about Jesus.”
Someone else becomes defensive. “Are you saying our parents and grandparents were wrong?”
And suddenly, a question about a holiday becomes a question about faith, family, obedience, and whether we have been honoring God or merely repeating what we inherited.
Perhaps you have been there.

Perhaps you grew up waiting for Christmas morning, singing hymns about the birth of Christ, attending Easter services, remembering the crucifixion during Holy Week, and believing that these celebrations were simply part of being a Christian.
Then one day, someone challenged you.
“Show me where Jesus commanded Christmas.”
You searched.
“Show me where the apostles commanded an annual Easter celebration.”
You searched again.
And the silence between the verses began to trouble you.

But before you throw away your decorations, condemn your church, accuse your family of paganism, or defend every tradition simply because it carries the name of Jesus, there is something we desperately need to understand.
The Bible does not command Christians to celebrate every religious holiday. But neither does it teach that every religious observance not explicitly commanded is automatically sinful.
And if we miss that distinction, we may end up fighting for biblical faithfulness while violating the very Scriptures we claim to defend.
This is not merely about Christmas.
This is not merely about Easter.
This is about who has the authority to bind your conscience.
And whether Jesus Christ is truly Lord over your worship.
Because sometimes the most dangerous tradition is not the one hanging on your calendar.
It is the one sitting unnoticed on the throne of your heart.
Consider the words of the apostle Paul.
In Romans 14:5–6, he writes:
Read that again.
One believer regards a particular day.
Another regards every day alike.
And Paul does not immediately pronounce one faithful and the other rebellious.
Instead, he directs attention toward the Lord.
In the original Greek, Romans 14:5 includes the expression:
ἕκαστος ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ νοῒ πληροφορείσθω
Hekastos en tō idiō noi plērophoreisthō.
A careful translation is:
“Let each one be fully convinced in his own mind.”
The Greek verb plērophoreisthō communicates being fully assured or convinced.
Paul is not encouraging careless religious individualism. He is not saying that every practice becomes acceptable simply because someone sincerely believes in it.
He is addressing a matter where believers differed over the observance of days and urging them to act with conviction before God rather than contempt toward one another.
The immediate context concerns disputable matters, including food and the observance of days. Paul is not specifically discussing modern Christmas or Easter celebrations.
Nevertheless, the passage gives us a principle that matters profoundly when evaluating religious observances Scripture has not commanded.
A Christian must not turn a matter of conscience into a universal command that God Himself has not given.
That truth cuts in both directions.
The believer who celebrates must not automatically condemn the believer who abstains.
And the believer who abstains must not automatically condemn the believer who celebrates.
Because Paul had already asked a piercing question in Romans 14:4:
“Who art thou that judgest another man's servant?”
Imagine standing before Jesus and discovering that you spent years attacking a brother who sincerely honored Christ on a particular day, while ignoring the pride growing inside your own heart.
Or imagine discovering that you pressured another believer to participate in a celebration that troubled their conscience, simply because you could not tolerate their refusal.
Both situations should make us uncomfortable.
Because Jesus never gave us permission to replace His authority with our preferences.
But there is another passage we cannot afford to ignore.
In Mark 7:6–8, Jesus confronts religious leaders whose traditions had begun to displace God's commandments.
He quotes Isaiah:
“This people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. Howbeit in vain do they worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.” (Mark 7:6–7, KJV)
Then He declares:
“For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men.” (Mark 7:8, KJV)
Those words should stop us.
Jesus was not impressed merely because a practice was old.
He was not impressed merely because respected religious leaders approved it.
He was not impressed merely because people called it worship.
The question was whether human tradition had displaced divine authority.
And that is where every Christian celebration must face an honest examination.
Not simply, “Did my family practice this?”
Not simply, “Does my church approve of it?”
Not even simply, “Does this make me feel close to God?”
But, “Does this practice honor Christ in a way consistent with His Word, or am I treating human customs as though God commanded them?”
There is a difference between remembering Jesus' birth and declaring that God requires every Christian to celebrate Christmas.
There is a difference between rejoicing in Christ's resurrection and insisting that every faithful believer must observe a particular annual holiday.
There is a difference between participating in a church tradition voluntarily and teaching that refusal to participate makes someone spiritually inferior.
And there is a difference between questioning a tradition and condemning everyone who practices it.
The distinction matters because the Gospel is not a religious calendar.
The Gospel is the good news of Jesus Christ—His incarnation, sinless life, atoning death, bodily resurrection, and saving grace received through faith.
Our salvation rests upon Christ, not upon our holiday observance.
Now consider Christmas.
Scripture clearly teaches that Jesus Christ was born.
Matthew and Luke record the extraordinary circumstances surrounding His birth. Luke 2:11 announces:
“For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord.” (KJV)
That is glorious truth.
The eternal Son entered human history.
The promised Messiah came.
The Savior was born.
But the New Testament does not command Christians to establish an annual celebration of His birth on December 25.
Nor does Scripture identify December 25 as His actual birthday.
The date became associated with Christian observance through later historical developments, and historians continue to discuss the factors behind its adoption.

Some popular claims about Christmas origins are much more confident than the historical evidence allows. It is inaccurate to assume that every Christmas custom has one simple pagan origin or that all Christian celebrations of December 25 arose through a single deliberate act of borrowing.
Historical questions deserve historical evidence.
Biblical questions deserve careful biblical interpretation.
And spiritual accusations deserve more than viral slogans.
The absence of a biblical command for Christmas does not, by itself, prove that remembering Christ's birth on a chosen day is sinful.
But neither does the importance of Christ's birth justify every activity associated with the holiday.

A celebration centered on generosity, thanksgiving, worship, and the truth of the incarnation is not spiritually identical to a celebration dominated by drunkenness, greed, deception, or neglect of the needy.
The name attached to a celebration does not sanctify everything done in it.
Which raises an uncomfortable question.
What if someone celebrates Christmas every year but rarely thinks about Christ outside December?
What if the decorations are magnificent, the gifts are expensive, the photographs are beautiful—but the family has no time for prayer, forgiveness, or Scripture?
What if we become furious when someone questions Christmas traditions, yet remain strangely calm when the commands of Jesus are neglected?
Perhaps the greater danger is not the calendar.
Perhaps it is a heart that knows how to celebrate Jesus without actually following Him.
Now consider Easter.
The resurrection of Jesus Christ is not an optional doctrine.
It stands at the center of Christianity.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 15:17:
Without the resurrection, Christianity collapses.
But Christ has risen.
The tomb was empty.
Death did not have the final word.
And every Christian has reason to rejoice.
Yet the New Testament does not issue a universal command requiring all Christians to observe an annual Easter Sunday according to a particular ecclesiastical calendar.

The history of Christian Pascha, often called Easter in English, is closely connected with the biblical Passover and early Christian remembrance of Christ's death and resurrection. Early Christians also differed over the timing of annual observances.
That history is more complicated than the popular claim that Easter is simply a pagan festival with a Christian label.
The English word Easter has its own linguistic history, while many Christian traditions use words derived from Pascha, connected to Passover.
The word's history alone cannot establish the spiritual meaning of every celebration bearing its name.
What matters is whether the actual practices are faithful to Christ.
A church may gather on an annual day to proclaim the resurrection without claiming that the date is a divine command.
Another believer may decline that annual observance while celebrating the risen Lord throughout the year.
Neither position, by itself, proves greater holiness.
But what about the holidays God actually commanded in Scripture?
This is where the discussion becomes even more important.
Leviticus 23 records appointed times given to Israel, including Passover, the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks, the Day of Atonement, and the Feast of Tabernacles.
The Hebrew expression used for appointed times is:
מוֹעֲדֵי יְהוָה
Mo'adei YHWH.
It means “the appointed times of the LORD.”
These were not merely cultural inventions. They were covenantal observances established by God for Israel.
Their significance should never be dismissed.
They reveal God's holiness, redemption, provision, and faithfulness. They also provide profound biblical context for understanding the ministry of Jesus Christ.
Paul declares in 1 Corinthians 5:7:
“For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us.” (KJV)
The Greek expression is:
τὸ πάσχα ἡμῶν ἐτύθη Χριστός
To pascha hēmōn etythē Christos.
A close rendering is:
“For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed.”
Paul identifies Jesus as the fulfillment of the Passover sacrifice's redemptive significance.
And Hebrews explains how Christ's priestly work and once-for-all sacrifice surpass the repeated sacrifices of the old covenant.
This does not make Israel's appointed feasts meaningless.
It means Christians must understand them through the finished work of Christ.
Under the new covenant, believers are not justified by observing Israel's ceremonial calendar.
Paul warns in Colossians 2:16–17:
“Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.” (KJV)
The Greek phrase:
τὸ δὲ σῶμα τοῦ Χριστοῦ
To de sōma tou Christou.
Can be rendered, in this context, “but the substance belongs to Christ,” or more literally, “but the body is of Christ.”
The contrast is between shadow and the reality to which the shadow points.
Christ is the center.
Christ is the fulfillment.
Christ is not an accessory to religious observance.
He is the One toward whom the redemptive story moves.
Christians differ over how particular biblical festivals and Sabbath principles should be practiced today. Those differences deserve careful study rather than caricature.
But one truth is unmistakable: no holiday observance can replace the saving work of Jesus.
And no celebration can accomplish what His blood has already accomplished.
Yet someone may ask, “Doesn't Deuteronomy warn against adopting pagan worship?”
Yes.
And we must take that warning seriously.
Deuteronomy 12:30–31 warns Israel not to imitate the detestable worship practices of the nations in serving the LORD.
The passage addresses real idolatrous practices, including horrific acts God condemned.
Christians must not worship idols, participate in occult rituals, or assume that an idolatrous act becomes acceptable merely because someone attaches Jesus' name to it.
Paul is equally clear in 1 Corinthians 10:14:
“Wherefore, my dearly beloved, flee from idolatry.” (KJV)
But we must be careful in applying these texts.
A historical resemblance between two customs does not automatically prove that everyone practicing a modern custom is worshiping a pagan deity.
The origin of a practice, its present meaning, the actions involved, and the participant's intentions all deserve examination.
Even good intentions cannot justify genuine idolatry.
But neither should uncertain historical associations be treated as conclusive proof of idolatry.
We cannot defend biblical truth by making claims the evidence cannot support.
And we cannot honor the God of truth by becoming careless with the truth.
There is another biblical event worth considering.
In John 10:22–23, Jesus is present in Jerusalem during the Feast of Dedication.
The Greek calls it:
τὰ ἐγκαίνια
Ta enkainia.
It refers to the Feast of Dedication, known today as Hanukkah.
This commemoration developed after the events recorded in the Hebrew Bible's Torah and commemorated the rededication of the Jerusalem temple.
John tells us that Jesus was at the temple during this festival.
That detail matters.
It demonstrates that a later religious commemoration could exist within the Jewish world in which Jesus ministered.
However, the passage does not explicitly say that Jesus endorsed every practice associated with the festival, nor does it command Christians to celebrate religious holidays of their own choosing.
It would be an overstatement to use His presence as blanket approval for every later Christian holiday.
But it would also be an overstatement to claim that Scripture presents every religious commemoration established after Moses as inherently sinful.
The biblical evidence calls for discernment, not simplistic slogans.
And perhaps that is what makes this subject so uncomfortable.
It refuses to give us an easy weapon against everyone who disagrees.
Some Christians want a verse that condemns every uncommanded holiday.
Others want a verse that blesses every cherished tradition.
But Scripture calls us to something more demanding.
Faithfulness.
Humility.
Truth.
Love.
A conscience shaped by God's Word.
And worship centered on Jesus Christ.
Now imagine two believers sitting in the same church.
One is a young mother who grew up in a home filled with anger.
Every December, her family gathers to read Luke 2, pray together, prepare meals for struggling neighbors, and remember the coming of Christ.
For her, the occasion has become an opportunity to teach her children about God's mercy.
Across the aisle sits a man who once practiced idolatrous religious rituals.
Certain seasonal customs remind him of the worship he abandoned when he surrendered his life to Jesus.
His conscience will not allow him to participate.
He does not want to return to anything that resembles his former bondage.
Both love Jesus.
Both want to obey Scripture.
Both are trying to act faithfully.
Now imagine the mother accusing the man of being legalistic because he abstains.
Imagine the man accusing the mother of being an idolater simply because she observes the day.
And imagine the grief of watching two people redeemed by the same Savior wound one another over a matter that requires careful discernment.
Romans 14:13 says:
“Let us not therefore judge one another any more: but judge this rather, that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother's way.” (KJV)
This is not permission to compromise with sin.
It is a command to exercise love where Scripture allows differences of conscience.
And that command is not optional.
We must distinguish between what God has forbidden, what God has commanded, and what God has left to responsible Christian judgment.
Because confusion between those categories has wounded families, divided churches, and turned sincere believers into enemies.
There is a special danger in religious pride.
It can wear the clothing of strictness.
And it can wear the clothing of freedom.
The strict believer may begin to think, “I am more faithful because I refuse what others celebrate.”
The permissive believer may begin to think, “I am more mature because I participate without guilt.”
Both can begin trusting their own position more than the grace of God.
And suddenly, the argument is no longer about honoring Jesus.
It is about winning.
Being right.
Feeling superior.
Proving that our group understands what everyone else has missed.
But the cross leaves no room for spiritual boasting.
Ephesians 2:8–9 reminds us:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (KJV)
You are not saved because you celebrate Christmas.
You are not saved because you refuse Christmas.
You are not saved because you observe Easter.
You are not saved because you reject Easter.
You are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And genuine saving faith bears fruit in a life increasingly shaped by obedience, repentance, love, and holiness.
That does not mean our choices are irrelevant.
It means our choices must flow from belonging to Christ rather than become substitutes for belonging to Him.
There is something deeply sobering about the way religious disputes can distract us from the commands we already understand.
Jesus commanded His disciples to love one another.
Have we obeyed?
He taught us to forgive.
Have we forgiven?
He told us to make disciples.
Are we making them?
He called us to deny ourselves, take up our cross, and follow Him.
Are we following?
He commanded us to remember Him in the breaking of bread.
Do we approach His sacrifice with reverence?
He taught us to care for those in need.
Are we caring?
He warned against hypocrisy.
Have we examined our own hearts?
We can spend hours debating whether a Christian should put up a Christmas tree while refusing to reconcile with someone we have wounded.
We can condemn commercialized holidays while allowing greed to control our everyday decisions.
We can insist that the resurrection should be celebrated every day while living as though the risen Christ has no authority over our speech, relationships, or secret habits.
And we can defend a beautiful church tradition while forgetting the Savior it was supposed to honor.
That is the tragedy.
We become experts at discussing the calendar while neglecting the Christ who rules over every day.
What would happen if we asked a different question?
Not merely, “Am I allowed to celebrate this?”
But, “Can I genuinely do this for the glory of God?”
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 10:31:
That principle reaches into every part of Christian life.
If you choose to observe a religious holiday, can you do so with gratitude to God, faithfulness to Scripture, integrity, and love?
Can you explain to your children the difference between biblical truth and human tradition?
Can you avoid treating customs as commands?
Can you refuse practices that involve sin or idolatry?
Can you celebrate without placing unnecessary burdens on your family or looking down on those who abstain?
And if you choose not to observe a religious holiday, can you abstain without pride?
Can you respect fellow believers whose consciences differ?
Can you explain your convictions without spreading unsupported accusations?
Can you remain gentle while holding firmly to Scripture?
Can you refuse to make your personal practice a test of salvation?
These questions are harder than simply declaring everyone else wrong.
Because they require us to examine ourselves.
And sometimes self-examination is more painful than argument.
Perhaps you are reading this while remembering a family disagreement.
A parent who felt rejected when you stopped participating in a celebration.
A child who felt condemned because you insisted on a tradition.
A spouse who became frustrated when your convictions changed.
A church friend who stopped speaking to you because you asked a sincere biblical question.
Perhaps words were spoken that cannot be taken back.
Perhaps you were called rebellious.
Perhaps you called someone deceived.
Perhaps what began as a desire to honor God became a battle that wounded people you love.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
You do not have to abandon biblical conviction to pursue reconciliation.
And you do not have to win every argument to remain faithful to Jesus.
You can say, “I still believe what I believe, but I am sorry for the way I treated you.”
You can say, “I cannot participate because of my conscience, but I do not want to condemn you unfairly.”
You can say, “I choose to observe this day, but I will not pressure you to join me.”
You can say, “I want us to open the Bible together instead of attacking each other.”
Sometimes repentance begins not with changing your conclusion, but with confessing the pride, harshness, or dishonesty that accompanied it.
And that kind of repentance is not weakness.
It is evidence that Christ is still transforming you.
Remember the thief on the cross.
He had no opportunity to build a religious calendar.
No years of holiday observances.
No impressive record of ceremonial faithfulness.
He turned to the crucified Jesus and said:
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” (Luke 23:42, KJV)
And Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” (Luke 23:43, KJV)
What saved that man?
Not a feast.
Not a festival.
Not a tradition.
Not his ability to settle every religious controversy.
His hope rested in the mercy and authority of the Savior beside him.
That does not make obedience unnecessary.
It reveals the foundation upon which all true obedience stands.
Grace.
The undeserved mercy of God in Jesus Christ.
The same Jesus who welcomed that dying sinner is the Jesus who calls us to repent, believe, and follow Him.
He does not invite us to replace obedience with religious sentiment.
And He does not invite us to replace grace with religious performance.
He calls us to Himself.
That is why the answer to our original question must remain anchored in Scripture.

Christians are not universally required to celebrate religious holidays that Scripture does not command. Yet the mere absence of an explicit command does not automatically make every voluntary religious commemoration sinful.
Such observances must be evaluated according to biblical teaching, the nature of the practices involved, the conscience of the believer, the good of others, and the glory of God.

A tradition becomes spiritually dangerous when it contradicts Scripture, encourages sin, displaces God's commandments, promotes idolatry, or is imposed as a divine requirement without biblical authority.
Likewise, rejecting a tradition becomes spiritually dangerous when abstinence turns into pride, false accusation, contempt, or a self-made standard of righteousness.
The issue is not whether we can invent a religious celebration and expect God to approve it automatically.
We cannot.
The issue is whether Scripture permits a particular voluntary remembrance without violating God's commands or binding the consciences of others.

Faithful Christians may reach different conclusions about particular observances, especially when they understand the historical background, associated practices, or relevant biblical principles differently.
Those differences should lead us deeper into Scripture, not further away from love.
And where a practice genuinely involves sin, we must refuse it, no matter how popular or traditional it becomes.
Jesus must have the final word.
Not nostalgia.
Not cultural pressure.
Not internet controversy.
Not denominational pride.
Not fear of disappointing people.
Jesus.
The One who was born in humility.
The One who lived without sin.
The One who was betrayed, mocked, beaten, and crucified.
The One who carried the judgment sinners deserved.
The One who rose bodily from the grave.
The One who will return in glory.
He is worthy of more than an annual celebration.
He is worthy of our lives.
And perhaps this is the question that should stay with us long after this article ends:
If every religious holiday disappeared tomorrow, would your devotion to Jesus remain?
Would you still open your Bible?
Would you still pray?
Would you still love your enemies?
Would you still forgive?
Would you still proclaim the Gospel?
Would you still worship when no special music was playing and no decorations were hanging?
Would you still follow Christ when obedience became costly?
Because the strongest evidence of genuine discipleship is not how passionately we defend a religious date.
It is whether our lives increasingly reflect the Lord we claim to honor.
There is room for sincere disagreement over certain observances.
There is no room for replacing Jesus with them.
And there is no excuse for forgetting the Gospel while arguing about how to remember it.

If this message has challenged something you have always believed, do not rush to defend yourself. Open the Scriptures. Read Romans 14, Mark 7, Colossians 2, 1 Corinthians 8–10, and Galatians 4 in their contexts. Ask God for wisdom. Examine your practices and your motives.
And if this exposed pride, fear, judgment, or confusion in your heart, you do not need to hide it.
Bring it to Jesus.
His grace is sufficient to forgive sinners, and His Word is sufficient to guide His people.
I want to invite you into an honest conversation, not a fight.

Or share your conviction respectfully: Do you celebrate religious holidays not explicitly commanded in Scripture, or do you choose to abstain? Which biblical passages have most shaped your understanding?
Your testimony may help someone who has been struggling silently with the same question.
There may be someone in your family who needs this conversation before another holiday becomes another argument.
There is also something personal I want to share with you.
Gospel Warrior is committed to helping people encounter the truth of Scripture, grow in the knowledge of Jesus Christ, and move beyond surface-level religion into genuine discipleship.
That work requires prayer, faithful service, time, resources, and people who believe biblical encouragement should continue reaching hearts beyond their own.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
That is the heart of this invitation.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not a promise that financial support purchases God's favor.
But an opportunity to participate willingly in a work you believe is helping people grow closer to Jesus.
Others can pray, share, encourage, or introduce someone to the Gospel.
All of those contributions matter.
That commitment to making biblical resources accessible remains an important part of the mission.
Keep growing in the Word.
Keep praying.
Keep sharing truth.
Keep pointing people to Jesus.
Because the goal has never been to build a community of people who merely agree about holidays.
The goal is to see lives transformed by the Gospel.
To see sinners repent.
To see the wounded find hope in Christ.
To see families reconciled.
To see believers become mature in Scripture.
To see people move from inherited religion to a living, obedient faith in the Savior.
And to see Jesus glorified—not merely on selected dates, but through lives surrendered to Him.
One day, the calendars we argued over will be forgotten.
The decorations will be packed away for the final time.
The songs of another season will fade.
The debates that seemed so enormous will fall silent.
And what will matter eternally is not whether we successfully defended every human tradition, but whether we truly belonged to Jesus Christ.
So celebrate with a clear conscience where Scripture permits.
Abstain with a clear conscience where conviction requires.
Never excuse what God calls sin.
Never command what God has not commanded.
Never let your freedom become an excuse for selfishness.
Never let your conviction become an excuse for pride.
And never forget the Savior while defending the celebration.
Because a holiday can remind you of Jesus.
But only Jesus can save you.
The tragedy would not be discovering that you celebrated the wrong day—it would be spending your life defending a day while never surrendering your heart to the Lord of every day.
